name: Meghalaya
blurb: The wettest place on Earth, where Khasi communities have grown living bridges from rubber-fig roots for over five centuries.

districts.name: East Khasi Hills
districts.blurb: Home to the double-decker living root bridges near Nongriat village.

places.name: Double-Decker Living Root Bridge
places.blurb: A bridge of two stacked levels, grown over generations by training the aerial roots of rubber fig trees across a gorge in Nongriat village.
places.bestPhoto: Midday, when light reaches the gorge floor through the canopy
places.history: War-Khasi communities began training Ficus elastica roots across streams centuries ago, guiding new growth through betel-nut trunk scaffolds until the roots fused into a load-bearing structure — a technique passed down orally between generations rather than recorded.
places.architecture: Unlike built bridges, a living root bridge strengthens with age; some in the region are over 100 years old and still growing. The double-decker at Nongriat is the most famous example, its two tiers formed decades apart.

timeline.label: Estimated founding growth of the lower deck.

facts: Some root bridges can bear the weight of 50 people at once.
They require no maintenance beyond periodic root-guiding.
Reaching it involves a steep 3,000-plus-step descent and climb.
hiddenGems: Rainbow Falls, a further 30-minute trek past the bridge
Village homestays in Nongriat run by Khasi families
Single-decker root bridges in nearby Riwai, an easier alternative
food: Jadoh (smoked pork rice) at village eateries
Fresh pineapple sold along the trail
experiences: Guided trek to the bridge and Rainbow Falls
Swimming in the natural rock pools below the bridge

travel.tip: Start the trek by 8 AM — the return climb is steep and best done before peak heat.

places.name: Nohkalikai Falls
places.blurb: India's tallest plunge waterfall, dropping around 340 metres off the Cherrapunji plateau into a pool whose colour changes with the rain.
places.bestPhoto: In or just after the monsoon, when the plunge pool is at its turquoise brightest
places.history: Named for Likai, a woman in a Khasi legend who jumped from the cliff in grief after a family tragedy; the pool below is said to be stained by it. The plateau behind it — Sohra, called Cherrapunji — is one of the wettest inhabited places on earth, and the fall is fed almost entirely by that rainfall, thinning to a thread in the dry months.
places.architecture: Shaped entirely by water: the plateau is a limestone formation, and the falls drop over an escarpment where the rock has been undercut over millennia. The result is a plunge fall rather than a cascade, with a deep, almost circular pool at the base that sits a long way from the viewing platform — which is why it reads as a single unbroken column of water.

timeline.label: Recorded as the wettest place on earth at neighbouring Cherrapunji.
Becomes a road-accessible viewpoint from the Sohra plateau.

facts: At roughly 340 metres it is India's tallest plunge waterfall.
Its pool shifts from blue to turquoise to green depending on rainfall.
In the driest months the flow can drop to a thin ribbon of water.
hiddenGems: The Mawsmai and Arwah limestone caves between Sohra town and the falls
Nohsngithiang (Seven Sisters) Falls, best seen in the monsoon
The Sohra plateau trail down toward the living root bridge at Nongriat
food: Jadoh and dohkhlieh at a Sohra eatery
Local honey and Sohra tea from roadside stalls
experiences: Photographing the falls in the monsoon when the flow is heaviest
Caving at Mawsmai, just a short drive away
Combining the falls with Mawlynnong and Riwai's root bridges on a full-day loop

travel.tip: Driving time from Shillong is short but the road climbs and winds — leave enough daylight for the return rather than the outbound.
